title: Azoth model spec
description: A calculation whose *algorithm* is the thing worth pinning down. A calc spec fixes an equation and both implementations evaluate it; a model spec fixes a procedure - a bracketing rule, a tolerance, an iteration cap - and both implementations run that procedure. The distinction matters because an iterated procedure that differs even slightly between two implementations diverges, and no check on the answer alone can tell a different-but-valid algorithm from the same one. Everything about units, quantities and bounds is `$ref`-ed from `calc.schema.json` rather than restated, so the two spec kinds share one definition of what a unit is.

id.description: Dotted identifier, e.g. eos.pure_saturation. Same rule as a calc id: it must match the module and function names in both implementations.

kind.description: What this model's spec fixes, and therefore whether it has an algorithm block. `procedure` - the usual case, and the reason the model tree exists at all - means a loop: a scheme, a convergence rule, a tolerance and a cap, which both implementations run and which a calc cannot express. `direct` means a computation over vectors with no iteration. A direct model is here because the calc registry's inputs are scalars, so a composition vector has nowhere to go; it has no `algorithm` block, and the schema forbids one rather than allowing a vacuous one, because a spec field nothing reads is the defect this project is organised against.

inputs.description: Input quantities, keyed by parameter name. A calc's inputs are all scalars; a model's may be vectors and matrices, because a mixture is a list of components rather than one number.

outputs.description: Output quantities, keyed by result field name.

cases.description: Cases both implementations must reproduce. The same idea as a calc's `tests`, minus the property tests: a property test is written against a calc's single equation, and a model's invariants are about its procedure - that the residual vanishes, that the bracket contains the answer - so they are written by hand in the test files and recorded in `assumptions` rather than declared here.

then.description: A procedure is a loop, and a loop needs its scheme, its convergence rule, its tolerance and its cap written down - that is the whole contract.

else.description: A direct model has no loop, so it must not carry an algorithm block. Forbidding one rather than ignoring it keeps `algorithm` meaning what it says: a thing both implementations run.

quantity.description: A scalar, vector or matrix quantity. A calc's `$defs.quantity` is `$ref`-ed rather than restated, so units and descriptions have one definition across both spec kinds; the two extra shapes exist because a mixture is not a number.

value.description: A case value: a number, a composition vector, or a matrix stated as rows. Extends the calc `$defs.value`, which permits a number or a list of *strings* - a model's vectors are numbers, and collecting them with the fitting-id rule gave a composition the type of a list of names.

length.description: What the length means, e.g. 'one entry per component'. Prose rather than a number, because the length is the caller's: the model is written for any N.

shape.description: The matrix's shape, e.g. 'N x N, symmetric, zero diagonal'. Recorded because a shape assertion a reader can check is worth more than one they assume.

algorithm.description: The procedure, stated completely enough that two implementations run the same one. This is the whole reason a model is not a calc: a calc's equation is a formula, and a model's is a loop, so the loop's stopping rule has to be written down somewhere both languages read.

scheme.description: The procedure's name, e.g. saturation_pressure_bisection. Held to the implementations by python/tests/models/test_model_contract.py, the way `solver.kind` is held by test_solver_contract.py. A scheme named here and implemented nowhere is the 'looks like validation, does nothing' failure this project exists to prevent.

initialisation.description: How the iteration starts, where the scheme needs a starting point. The analogue of a solver's `initial_guess`, and in the spec for the same reason: two implementations that start from different guesses take different paths to the same answer, and a convergence claim that holds from one starting point need not hold from another. `wilson` is the K-value correlation.

inner.description: A nested procedure the outer one runs each iteration. Recursive, because an inner scheme has the same shape as an outer one and describing it with a second set of keys would be a second definition of what an algorithm is.

initial_temperature.description: Where a quasi-Newton inversion of a property starts, in kelvin. The isentropic and isenthalpic flashes iterate from a temperature rather than bracketing one, so it has to be declared: two implementations starting from different temperatures take different paths, and a convergence claim that holds from one need not hold from another. Upstream starts from the temperature its thermodynamic system already holds - for a compressor, the inlet temperature - and a model here has no system, so the spec states the start instead.

bracket.description: How the interval the iteration starts from is found. Part of the scheme rather than an implementation detail: two implementations that bracket differently find different roots when there is more than one, and the difference is invisible in the converged answer until it is a different answer.

lower.description: Where the search starts, in the reduced variable the scheme names - dimensionless, like everything else in a model's interior, so the bracket does not depend on which unit a caller used.

steps.description: How many points the search evaluates. Stated because it quantises the bracket: the interval the iteration then refines is only as tight as this step size, and two implementations with different step counts take different numbers of iterations to the same answer.

inputs.description: Input values in the units declared in `inputs`, exactly as a calc's worked example states them - except that a vector or matrix input is stated as an array, since a mixture has no scalar form.
